title: The 7 Money Levels: Where Are You in 2027?

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Every person watching this video is on one of seven money levels. Not because of how much they earn, but because of what their money is doing right now. Some people are fighting debt every month. Some people never have to work again. And most people are stuck somewhere in the middle without knowing which level they're on, or what it takes to move up.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: There are seven money levels. Most people are stuck on level two.

scenes.text: Seven levels. From owing more than you own, all the way to money that pays for your whole life. By the end of this video you'll know exactly where you are, and the one move that gets you to the next level.

Here's the surprising part. Your level has very little to do with your salary. There are doctors on level one, buried in debt, and there are mechanics and teachers on level six. Income helps, of course. But the level you're on is decided by what happens to your money after it arrives.
scenes.caption: IT'S NOT YOUR SALARY

scenes.text: And each level has its own trap. A mistake that feels completely normal at that level, but keeps people stuck there for years. We'll look at all seven traps, with real numbers from the Federal Reserve and other named sources, so you can skip the mistakes most people make.
scenes.caption: EVERY LEVEL HAS A TRAP

scenes.text: So let's find out where you are. Grab a piece of paper, or just keep count in your head. Let's start at the bottom.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Quick note on the data. Net worth numbers come from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, the most detailed study of American household wealth, published every three years. The latest full survey covers twenty twenty two. We also use the Federal Reserve's survey on household well being, Bankrate's savings research, and the New York Fed's report on household debt.
scenes.query: Federal Reserve Bank of New York building
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: When we show growth over time, we use a seven percent average yearly return as an illustration. That is not a promise. Real markets go up and down, sometimes a lot. This video is education, not financial advice. Use it to understand the map, then make decisions that fit your own life.
scenes.query: Calculator and pen on financial papers
scenes.caption: EDUCATION, NOT ADVICE

scenes.text: First, the big picture. According to the Federal Reserve, the median American family had a net worth of about one hundred ninety two thousand dollars in twenty twenty two. Median means half had more, half had less. But the average was over one million dollars, pulled up by the very top.

card.note: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022

scenes.text: That gap tells you something important. The average is misleading. Most families are much closer to the median, and a big share of that median is home equity, money you can't easily spend. So if your number feels small, you are probably more normal than you think.
scenes.caption: THE AVERAGE LIES

scenes.text: Age matters a lot too. The same survey found the median net worth for families under thirty five was about thirty nine thousand dollars. For thirty five to forty four, about one hundred thirty five thousand. For forty five to fifty four, about two hundred forty seven thousand.

card.note: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022

scenes.text: Keep those numbers in mind, because they'll help you see where you really stand. Now, level one.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Level one. Underwater. You owe more than you own. Your net worth is below zero. If you sold everything you have today, you still couldn't pay off what you owe.

card.title: Underwater
card.sub: you owe more than you own

scenes.caption: LEVEL 1
scenes.short_hook: If you pay only the minimum on your credit card, watch this.

scenes.text: Level one usually looks like this. Credit card balances that never really go down. A car loan bigger than what the car is worth. Student loans. Maybe a buy now pay later plan or two. Every month, a big part of the paycheck is already spoken for before it even arrives.
scenes.caption: DEBT EVERYWHERE

scenes.text: And it's more common than people admit. The New York Fed reports that Americans owe more than eighteen trillion dollars in household debt, including well over one trillion on credit cards alone. Credit card interest rates have been above twenty percent, which means a balance can grow faster than most people can pay it down.
scenes.query: Federal Reserve Bank of New York building
scenes.caption: $18 TRILLION OWED

scenes.text: The trap at level one is paying the minimum and feeling like you're making progress. On a card charging over twenty percent, the minimum payment mostly covers interest. You can pay for years and still owe almost the same amount. It feels responsible. It's actually treading water.
scenes.caption: THE MINIMUM PAYMENT TRAP

scenes.text: The move to level two is simple, not easy. List every debt with its interest rate. Stop adding new debt. Then throw every extra dollar at the highest rate first, while paying the minimum on the rest. When one is gone, roll that payment into the next one. That's the fastest way up.
scenes.caption: HIGHEST RATE FIRST

scenes.text: Level two. Paycheck to paycheck. You're not sinking anymore, but you're not moving either. Your net worth is around zero, and your bank account hits nearly zero right before every payday.

card.title: Paycheck to paycheck
card.sub: zero at the end of every month

scenes.caption: LEVEL 2

scenes.text: Level two is where a huge number of Americans live, including people with good incomes. The money comes in, and somehow it all goes out. Rent, car, groceries, subscriptions, a dinner out. Nothing crazy. But nothing left over, either.
scenes.caption: NOTHING LEFT OVER

scenes.text: The Federal Reserve found that sixty three percent of adults would cover a surprise four hundred dollar expense with cash. That means more than a third would not. And Bankrate found that about one in four Americans has no emergency savings at all. At level two, one flat tire can push you right back to level one.
scenes.query: Car with flat tire on road
scenes.caption: ONE FLAT TIRE

scenes.text: The trap at level two is lifestyle creep. Every raise disappears. A bigger apartment, a nicer car, more eating out. Each upgrade feels earned, and it is. But if your spending rises as fast as your income, you stay on level two forever, just with nicer things.
scenes.caption: LIFESTYLE CREEP

scenes.text: The move to level three is to pay yourself first. Set up an automatic transfer of even fifty dollars on payday, into a separate savings account, before you can spend it. Then, the next time you get a raise, send at least half of it to that account. Your lifestyle still improves, and your savings finally start.
scenes.caption: PAY YOURSELF FIRST

scenes.text: Level three. The starter cushion. You have somewhere between one thousand and ten thousand dollars saved. A surprise bill is annoying, but it's not a crisis anymore.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 3

scenes.text: Level three feels different. The car repair, the vet bill, the urgent flight home, you can pay them. You don't have to borrow, and you don't have to ask anyone for help. That alone takes a weight off your shoulders that most people don't even realize they're carrying.
scenes.caption: NOT A CRISIS ANYMORE

scenes.text: Here's how close this level really is. Saving five hundred dollars a month gets you to ten thousand dollars in twenty months. Two hundred fifty a month gets you there in under three and a half years. It isn't magic. It's just a transfer that happens every single month without you thinking about it.
scenes.caption: 20 MONTHS TO $10,000

scenes.text: The trap at level three is raiding the cushion for things that aren't emergencies. A sale, a vacation, a new phone. Then the real emergency arrives and the money's gone. The fix is to keep it in a separate account, ideally at a different bank, so spending it takes a deliberate decision.
scenes.caption: DON'T RAID THE CUSHION

scenes.text: The move to level four is to grow the cushion to three to six months of essential costs, and keep it in a high yield savings account. Then, once it's full, start investing a regular amount every month, even a small one. That's the moment your money starts working, not just sitting.
scenes.caption: SEPARATE ACCOUNT

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you've already found your level, I'd love to know which one. Tell me in the comments. And if this is helping you, subscribe to the channel. It's free, and it helps me keep making these videos for you.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Level four. Stable. Your emergency fund is full, your high interest debt is gone, and you're investing every month. Your net worth is somewhere between ten thousand and one hundred thousand dollars.

card.title: Stable
card.sub: a real safety net and money invested

scenes.caption: LEVEL 4

scenes.text: This is where life gets calmer. A layoff would hurt, but you'd have months to recover. You're not checking your balance before every purchase. And for the first time, you're putting money into investments like broad index funds or a retirement account, on purpose, every single month.
scenes.caption: LIFE GETS CALMER

scenes.text: At level four, your own contributions do almost all the work. If you invest three hundred dollars a month for ten years, at a seven percent average yearly return, you'd have roughly fifty two thousand dollars. You put in thirty six thousand. The rest is growth, and it's only getting started.
scenes.caption: YOUR MONEY STARTS WORKING

scenes.text: The trap at level four is getting impatient. The growth feels slow, so people chase faster money. Hot stocks, crypto tips, a friend's business idea. Some of it might work. Most of it costs people years. At this level, boring and consistent beats exciting almost every time.
scenes.caption: DON'T CHASE FAST MONEY

scenes.text: The move to level five is to raise your savings rate. Not just your income, your rate. Try going from ten percent of your income to fifteen, then twenty. Use every raise, every bonus, and every paid off loan to push it higher. That's what gets you to one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: RAISE YOUR SAVINGS RATE

scenes.text: Level five. Momentum. Your net worth is between one hundred thousand and about five hundred thousand dollars. This is where your money starts to pull its own weight.

card.title: Momentum
card.sub: your money starts doing real work

scenes.caption: LEVEL 5

scenes.text: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime partner, famously said the first one hundred thousand dollars is the hardest. Here's why. At seven percent, one hundred thousand dollars can grow by around seven thousand dollars in a single year, without you adding anything. That's a real raise you didn't have to ask for.
scenes.caption: THE HARDEST $100,000

scenes.text: And it compounds. One hundred thousand dollars plus one thousand dollars a month, at a seven percent average yearly return, reaches one million dollars in about twenty one years. That isn't a promise, markets vary, but it shows how level five turns into level six with patience.
scenes.query: New York Stock Exchange trading floor
scenes.caption: COMPOUNDING KICKS IN

scenes.text: The trap at level five is fees and lifestyle. A one percent yearly fee doesn't sound like much, but on a growing portfolio it can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars over a lifetime. And this is the level where people upgrade their house and car, and lock in costs that slow everything down.
scenes.caption: FEES AND BIG UPGRADES

scenes.text: The move to level six is to protect the machine. Keep your fees low, keep investing through market drops, and keep your big fixed costs under control. Most people who reach level six didn't do anything brilliant. They just didn't interrupt the process.
scenes.caption: PROTECT THE MACHINE

scenes.text: Level six. Millionaire. Your net worth has passed one million dollars. It sounds like the finish line. For most people who get here, it isn't.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 6
scenes.short_hook: One million dollars is not the finish line. Here's why.

scenes.text: UBS's Global Wealth Report estimates there are more than twenty million millionaires in the United States. Most of them are not celebrities. They're often people in their fifties and sixties who owned a home for decades, saved in retirement accounts, and never stopped. Many of them drive ordinary cars.
scenes.caption: QUIET MILLIONAIRES

scenes.text: Here's the reality check. One million dollars sounds rich, but if half of it is your home, the money you could actually live on is much smaller. Using the four percent rule of thumb, five hundred thousand dollars in investments supports about twenty thousand dollars a year. Nice, but not freedom yet.
scenes.caption: $1 MILLION IS NOT FREEDOM YET

scenes.text: The trap at level six is feeling rich and acting like it. Bigger house, second home, expensive hobbies. At this level, a few large decisions can easily erase ten years of progress. The people who stay here keep their spending tied to what their investments can really support.
scenes.caption: DON'T ACT RICH

scenes.text: The move to level seven is to stop measuring net worth and start measuring one thing: how many years of your life your investments can pay for. That changes every decision. Suddenly a cheaper house isn't a sacrifice. It's years of your freedom bought back.
scenes.caption: COUNT YEARS, NOT DOLLARS

scenes.text: Level seven. Financially independent. Your investments can pay for your life, indefinitely. Work becomes a choice, not a requirement.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 7

scenes.text: A common rule of thumb comes from research by financial planner William Bengen in the nineteen nineties: withdrawing about four percent in the first year, then adjusting for inflation, has historically lasted at least thirty years in most periods. Flip that around, and you need about twenty five times your yearly spending.
scenes.caption: THE 4% RULE

scenes.text: So the number is personal. If you spend forty thousand dollars a year, you need about one million dollars invested. If you spend eighty thousand, you need about two million. That's why spending less is so powerful. It lowers the finish line and gets you there faster at the same time.
scenes.caption: 25 TIMES YOUR SPENDING

scenes.text: The trap at level seven is assuming the rule is a guarantee. It isn't. A bad market right at the start of retirement, high inflation, or big health costs can change the math. Most people at this level keep some flexibility, like spending a little less in bad years, or earning a bit on the side.
scenes.caption: NOT A GUARANTEE

scenes.text: And here's what people at level seven say surprised them most. It wasn't the money. It was the time. Time with family, time to build something they care about, time to say no. That's what all seven levels are really about. Not getting rich. Getting free.
scenes.caption: IT'S ABOUT TIME

scenes.text: Now let's look at these seven levels from three different angles. First the numbers, then the psychology, then the playbook. Because knowing your level is one thing. Understanding why people get stuck there, and exactly what to do about it, is what actually moves you up.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Angle 1: The numbers behind each level

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. The biggest number on every level isn't your salary. It's the gap between what comes in and what goes out. Economists call it your savings rate. If you earn four thousand dollars a month after tax and spend three thousand six hundred, your savings rate is ten percent. If you spend three thousand two hundred, it's twenty percent. That one number decides how fast you climb, more than any investment you will ever pick.
scenes.query: Calculator and pen on financial papers
scenes.caption: THE GAP DECIDES EVERYTHING

scenes.text: Here's what the gap does over time. Two hundred dollars a month, invested for thirty years at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly two hundred forty four thousand dollars. Double it to four hundred a month, and it's roughly four hundred eighty eight thousand. Same person, same market. The only difference is the gap.

card.note: Illustration, compounded monthly. Returns are not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Now look at the math of debt, because it works in exactly the same way, just backwards. A five thousand dollar credit card balance at twenty two percent costs about eleven hundred dollars a year in interest. That's eleven hundred dollars that could have been invested, and instead it went to the bank. On level one, compound interest is working against you every single day. The first goal is simply to switch sides.
scenes.caption: COMPOUNDING IN REVERSE

scenes.text: Here's another number that matters on levels two and three: months of runway. Take the money you could reach in a week, and divide it by what you spend in a month on essentials. Rent, food, transport, insurance, minimum payments. If the answer is under one, any surprise becomes debt. Between one and three, you can absorb most surprises. Over three to six, a job loss becomes a hard time instead of a disaster.
scenes.caption: MONTHS OF RUNWAY

scenes.text: On levels four and five, the number that starts to matter is the one most people never calculate: what their money earned this year compared with what they added. In the early years, almost all of the growth is your own contributions. But somewhere around the middle of level five, at a seven percent illustration, a typical year of growth can match a year of saving. That's the crossover point, and you can see it on your own statements.
scenes.caption: THE CROSSOVER POINT

scenes.text: And on levels six and seven, the number is years of freedom. Divide your investments by your yearly spending. Five hundred thousand dollars invested and forty thousand a year in spending is twelve and a half years. One million at the same spending is twenty five years, which is the old four percent rule of thumb. It's not a perfect measure, but it's the most honest one, because it ties your money to your actual life.
scenes.caption: YEARS OF FREEDOM

scenes.text: Put those together and you get a simple scorecard you can fill in on one piece of paper. Your savings rate. Your months of runway. Your growth compared with your contributions. And your years of freedom. Those four numbers tell you your level more accurately than any salary or any bank balance ever could. And the good news is, every one of them can be improved starting this month.
scenes.caption: YOUR 4-NUMBER SCORECARD

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Because if money were only math, everybody would be on level five. It isn't. Every level has its own way of thinking, and the way of thinking is usually what keeps people stuck.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Angle 2: The psychology of each level
scenes.short_hook: Why do people with good salaries stay broke? It's not math.

scenes.text: On level one, the feeling is shame, and shame makes people look away. They stop opening statements. They don't know their exact balances. And what you don't look at, you can't fix. Researchers Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir wrote about this in their book Scarcity. When money is very tight, your mind narrows onto the urgent problem in front of you, and long term planning gets squeezed out. It's not a character flaw. It's what scarcity does to anyone.
scenes.caption: SCARCITY NARROWS YOUR MIND

scenes.text: So the fix on level one is not willpower. It's making the problem small and visible. One list. Every debt, every balance, every rate. People are often surprised that once the list exists, the anxiety drops, even before a single dollar is paid. The monster under the bed is always bigger than the monster on paper.
scenes.caption: MAKE IT VISIBLE

scenes.text: On level two, the mindset is, I deserve it. And honestly, you probably do. You work hard. But the problem is that every purchase gets judged on its own, and almost any single purchase looks reasonable. The coffee, the delivery, the upgrade. Behavioral economists call this mental accounting. We put money in different mental buckets, and we don't see the total. Level two people rarely have one big leak. They have thirty small ones.
scenes.caption: THIRTY SMALL LEAKS

scenes.text: On level three, the feeling shifts to relief, and relief brings a new risk: comfort. You've got a few thousand dollars, the pressure's off, and it's tempting to stop. This is the level where many people stall for years. Not because they can't save more, but because the urgency is gone. The trick is to replace fear with a goal. Not, I need money. But, I want ten thousand dollars by next summer.
scenes.caption: RELIEF BECOMES COMFORT

scenes.text: On level four, the enemy is boredom. Investing every month in a broad fund is not exciting. Nothing happens most days. So people start tinkering. They check prices daily, they move money around, they chase whatever went up last month. Studies of investor behavior, like the long running research by the firm DALBAR, have repeatedly found that the average investor earns less than the funds they invest in, largely because of bad timing.
scenes.caption: BORING IS THE POINT

scenes.text: On level five, the mindset is comparison. Your friends upgrade their houses. Your coworker buys a new truck. Social media shows you people your age on beaches every weekend. And because you now have real money, you can afford to keep up, at least for a while. Psychologists sometimes call this the hedonic treadmill. Every upgrade feels great for a few months, then it becomes normal, and you need the next one.
scenes.caption: THE HEDONIC TREADMILL

scenes.text: On level six, the risk is overconfidence. You did it once, so you start believing you can't lose. People take bigger bets, put too much money in one stock or one deal, or lend to someone with a great story. And on level seven, the surprising feeling is often fear. People who saved for decades find it hard to actually spend. Some keep working long after they need to, just because spending feels wrong.
scenes.caption: OVERCONFIDENCE AND FEAR

scenes.text: So here's the pattern. Shame, then entitlement, then comfort, boredom, comparison, overconfidence, and finally fear. Every level has a feeling that pulls you sideways. If you know which feeling belongs to your level, you can see it coming. And seeing it coming is half the battle.
scenes.caption: SEE IT COMING

scenes.text: Angle three. The playbook. Here's exactly what I'd do this week on each level. Not someday. This week. Find yours and do just the steps for your level.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Angle 3: The playbook for each level
scenes.short_hook: Do these three things this week to move up one money level.

scenes.text: Level one, this week. Write the list of every debt with its balance and interest rate. Cancel or pause any subscription you didn't use last month. Call your credit card company and ask for a lower interest rate. It doesn't always work, but it costs nothing to ask. And pick your target: the highest rate debt, which gets every extra dollar from now on.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 1: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Level two, this week. Open a separate savings account, ideally at a different bank from your checking. Set an automatic transfer on payday, even twenty five or fifty dollars. Then look at your last month of spending and circle every purchase you don't remember making. Those are your leaks. Pick three to stop.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 2: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Level three, this week. Write down your essential monthly costs and multiply by three. That's your next target. Move your cushion to a high yield savings account if it's earning almost nothing. Rates change, so compare a few banks, and check that the bank is FDIC insured. And give the account a name, like Freedom Fund. It sounds silly, but named goals are harder to raid.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 3: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Level four, this week. If your employer offers a retirement plan with a match, make sure you're contributing at least enough to get the full match. That's part of your pay you're leaving on the table otherwise. Then set your investing on autopilot, and turn off daily price notifications. Check your investments once a month, at most.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 4: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Level five, this week. Find the expense ratio of every fund you own and add up what you pay in dollars per year. Then write down your three biggest fixed costs: housing, cars, insurance. Before any upgrade to one of them, ask a simple question. How many months of freedom does this cost me? Sometimes it's worth it. Often it isn't.
scenes.caption: LEVEL 5: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Level six, this week. Check that no single stock, property or business is so large that losing it would drop you two levels. Review your insurance and your will, or start one if you don't have it. And level seven, this week. Write a simple spending plan for the next twelve months, including a version for a bad market year. Then, and this is the hard part, plan something to actually enjoy.
scenes.caption: LEVELS 6 AND 7: THIS WEEK

scenes.text: Notice something about this playbook. None of it requires a high income. None of it requires predicting the stock market. It's lists, automatic transfers, a few phone calls and a few rules. That's the honest truth about money levels. The people at the top mostly did simple things for a long time.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE THINGS, LONG TIME

scenes.text: So how long does it actually take to climb? Let me show you the math, because it's more encouraging than you think.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's one path. Five hundred dollars a month, invested for thirty years at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly six hundred ten thousand dollars. You'd put in one hundred eighty thousand. More than two thirds of the final number is growth.

Now double the effort. One thousand dollars a month for twenty five years, at the same seven percent illustration, grows to roughly eight hundred ten thousand dollars. You'd put in three hundred thousand. Higher contributions shorten the climb by years.

The pattern is always the same. The first levels are about behavior: stopping debt, saving on autopilot, building a cushion. The middle levels are about consistency: investing every month and not interrupting it. And the top levels are about protection: low fees, controlled spending, and patience.
scenes.caption: BEHAVIOR, CONSISTENCY, PROTECTION

scenes.text: And here's the part people forget. You don't have to climb all seven levels to change your life. Going from level one to level three, from debt to a real cushion, is the biggest jump in peace of mind most people will ever feel. Start there.
scenes.caption: START WITH THE NEXT LEVEL

scenes.text: Numbers are easier to feel when they belong to a person. So here are three example climbs. These are made up examples, not real people, but every number in them is simple math you can check.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Example one. Maria is twenty six, earns forty eight thousand dollars a year, and owes nine thousand dollars on two credit cards. She's on level one. She writes her list, stops using the cards, and finds three hundred fifty dollars a month by cutting delivery food and switching her phone plan. Her minimum payments were about two hundred fifty dollars, so now six hundred dollars a month goes at the debt, highest rate card first. At around twenty two percent interest, she's debt free in about a year and a half.
scenes.caption: EXAMPLE 1: MARIA

scenes.text: Then the magic part. The moment her last card is paid, she doesn't spend that money. She keeps the same payment going, but now into her own savings account. In about a year, she has a cushion of around seven thousand dollars, with a bit of interest on top. At twenty eight, she's on level three. Same salary. Same apartment. Completely different life.
scenes.caption: SAME SALARY, NEW LEVEL

scenes.text: Example two. James and Tasha are thirty five, with two kids and a combined income of ninety five thousand dollars. They're on level two: no debt except the mortgage and one car loan, but nothing left at the end of each month. When the car loan ends, they keep driving the car and redirect the four hundred fifty dollar payment. They also send half of every raise to savings.
scenes.caption: EXAMPLE 2: JAMES AND TASHA

scenes.text: Within two years they have a full emergency fund. Then they start investing six hundred dollars a month. At a seven percent illustration, that grows to roughly one hundred four thousand dollars in ten years, on top of their home equity. By their mid forties, they're solidly on level five. Nobody around them noticed anything, because they never changed the way they lived. They just stopped upgrading.
scenes.caption: THEY STOPPED UPGRADING

scenes.text: Example three. Robert is fifty two. He has about one hundred fifty thousand dollars in a retirement account and a paid off house, so he's on level five, but he's worried he started too late. He's in his peak earning years, so he raises his contributions to fifteen hundred dollars a month for the next thirteen years.
scenes.caption: EXAMPLE 3: ROBERT

scenes.text: At a seven percent illustration, his one hundred fifty thousand plus those contributions could grow to roughly seven hundred fifty thousand dollars by sixty five. Add Social Security, and a paid off house, and his level seven number, the amount he needs, is much smaller than he feared. Late isn't the same as never. It just means your monthly number does more of the work.
scenes.caption: LATE IS NOT NEVER

scenes.text: Look at what these three examples have in common. Nobody won the lottery. Nobody picked a magic stock. Each one found a gap, protected it with an automatic transfer, and refused to let lifestyle creep eat it. The level changed because the behavior changed, and the behavior changed because the money became visible.
scenes.caption: WHAT THEY HAD IN COMMON

scenes.text: Climbing is one thing. Not falling back down is another. Here are five mistakes that knock people down a level, sometimes two.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Five mistakes that drop you a level

scenes.text: Mistake one. No emergency fund once you start investing. When the surprise comes, people sell investments at a bad time or go back to credit cards. Mistake two. A car payment that's too big. Cars lose value fast, and a large loan can drag you from level four back to level two.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES ONE AND TWO

scenes.text: Mistake three. Panic selling in a market drop. Broad markets have fallen twenty percent or more many times, and recovered, though past results don't guarantee the future. Selling at the bottom turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss. Mistake four. Co-signing loans for friends or family. If they don't pay, you do.
scenes.query: Stock market chart falling on screen
scenes.caption: MISTAKES THREE AND FOUR

scenes.text: And mistake five. Falling for a scam or a too good to be true investment. The Federal Reserve found that about one in five adults experienced fraud or a scam in a single year. The higher your level, the more of a target you become. If someone promises guaranteed high returns, walk away.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE FIVE: SCAMS

scenes.text: Before the recap, let me answer the questions I get the most about these levels.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Does my home count? For net worth, yes. Your home's value minus your mortgage is part of it. But for these levels, I'd look mostly at money you can actually use: savings and investments. A big house with no savings is still level two in daily life.
scenes.caption: DOES MY HOME COUNT?

scenes.text: Question two. Can I skip a level? Not really. People try to jump from level two straight to investing big, without a cushion. Then the first emergency sends them back down. Each level builds the floor for the next one. Question three. Is it too late at fifty? No. Your monthly savings need to do more of the work, but people in their fifties often earn the most they ever will.
scenes.caption: SKIP A LEVEL? TOO LATE?

scenes.text: Question four. What if I have a low income? Then the early levels are about protecting what you have. Avoid high interest debt, build even a small cushion, and look for ways to raise your income, like new skills or a better paying job. Small amounts still count, because the habit is what moves you up.
scenes.caption: LOW INCOME?

scenes.text: Question five. Should I invest or pay off debt first? It depends on the interest rate. Debt above roughly eight to ten percent, like most credit cards, usually comes first, because paying it off is a guaranteed return at that rate. Low rate debt, like some mortgages, can sit alongside investing. And in almost every case, grab any employer match first, because that's an instant return you won't find anywhere else.
scenes.caption: DEBT OR INVEST FIRST?

scenes.text: Question six. How often should I check my level? Once a month is plenty for most people. Pick the same day, maybe the first Sunday of the month. Write down your four numbers: savings rate, months of runway, growth compared with contributions, and years of freedom. Checking every day makes you react to noise. Checking once a month shows you the trend, and the trend is what matters.
scenes.caption: CHECK ONCE A MONTH

scenes.text: Let's recap. Level one, underwater, you owe more than you own. Level two, paycheck to paycheck. Level three, the starter cushion. Level four, stable, with a full emergency fund and regular investing.
scenes.caption: LEVELS 1 TO 4

scenes.text: Level five, momentum, where your money does real work. Level six, millionaire, which isn't the finish line. And level seven, financially independent, when your investments can pay for your life and work becomes optional.
scenes.caption: LEVELS 5 TO 7

scenes.text: And remember the three angles. The numbers: your savings rate, your runway, your growth and your years of freedom. The psychology: shame, entitlement, comfort, boredom, comparison, overconfidence and fear, one feeling for each level, pulling you sideways. And the playbook: a few simple moves this week, for your level only. If you remember nothing else from this video, remember that your level is not a verdict on you as a person. It's just a starting point on a map, and every level on that map has a path to the next one. Millions of people have walked it before you, most of them with ordinary jobs and ordinary incomes.
scenes.caption: NUMBERS, PSYCHOLOGY, PLAYBOOK

scenes.text: Now pick your level and do just one thing: the move to the next one. That's it. If you want the full plan, step by step, it's in my playbook. The link is in the description. And if you're on level three or four, watch my video on what changes at one hundred thousand dollars. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
